# Rule catalogue

Every rule `dpa-review` runs, generated from the rules in [`src/dpa_review/checks.py`](../src/dpa_review/checks.py). A finding is open when its status is `MISSING` or `NEEDS_REVIEW`. Any open `HIGH` finding makes the packet `BLOCKED` (exit `2`); any other open finding makes it `NEEDS_REVIEW` (exit `1`); otherwise it is `CLEARED_FOR_REVIEW` (exit `0`), which still needs a lawyer's sign-off. Input keys are described in [input-format.md](input-format.md).

## Transfer rules by basis

`transfer.<country>` checks each direct destination and `transfer.subprocessor.<name>` each sub-processor outside the EEA. Both use the same assessment of the country and the recorded mechanism (status and severity). The table shows each mechanism with nothing else recorded: for `dpf`, no certification on the Data Privacy Framework List; for `derogation_art49`, a transfer not recorded as occasional and not repetitive; for an Art. 46 safeguard, no transfer impact assessment. Art. 46(1) makes the safeguards the transfer basis only in the absence of an adequacy decision, so a safeguard recorded for a destination with a decision is not needed where the decision covers the importer. Where the decision's scope turns on facts about the importer (Canada, Israel, Japan, Korea; see [Scope conditions](#scope-conditions)), the recorded facts decide: a failed condition means the decision does not cover the importer, and an unknown one never counts as adequacy, so a transfer recorded as relying on the decision is `NEEDS_REVIEW` (`HIGH`) until the facts are recorded. With a safeguard recorded, the finding asks whether the importer is within the decision, or says it is not and the safeguard carries the transfer; once a transfer impact assessment is recorded that finding is LOW instead of MEDIUM. Brazil and the Faroe Islands have a scope limit the input records no fact for: a transfer on the decision is read as covered and the finding asks the reviewer to confirm the limit, and a safeguard gets the same question. The United States has a decision that covers only organisations on the Data Privacy Framework List (Implementing Decision (EU) 2023/1795), so a safeguard recorded for the US gets the same question, about that list. With a `review_date`, each decision is read as it applied on that date (see [Reference data](#reference-data)).

## Reference data

The destination lists the transfer rules use, as they stand in `checks.py`. Every adequacy decision below rests on its Official Journal text, snapshotted under [`sources/oj`](../sources/oj) with its URL, retrieval date and SHA-256 in [`sources/manifest.json`](../sources/manifest.json); `tests/test_adequacy.py` checks each number, date, Official Journal reference and operative provision against the snapshot. The table is as at 2026-11-14: on that date every snapshot was re-fetched and found unchanged, and the Publications Office's Cellar was searched for later adequacy acts (`dpa-review-table-age` reports its age). The EUR-Lex records of status and amendments were read on 2026-11-10. Decisions are amended, extended and adopted after these dates: re-check the decision on EUR-Lex before relying on a result.

- EEA (30): AT, BE, BG, CY, CZ, DE, DK, EE, ES, FI, FR, GR, HR, HU, IE, IS, IT, LI, LT, LU, LV, MT, NL, NO, PL, PT, RO, SE, SI, SK
- Adequacy (Art. 45) (16): AD, AR, BR, CA, CH, EPO, FO, GB, GG, IL, IM, JE, JP, KR, NZ, UY

| NZ | New Zealand | [Commission Implementing Decision 2013/65/EU](https://eur-lex.europa.eu/legal-content/EN/TXT/?uri=CELEX:32013D0065) of 19 December 2012, Art. 1(1), in force under Art. 45(9) | OJ L 28, 30.1.2013, p. 12 | 19 December 2012 (adoption date, see note) | no end date | none | none |
| UY | Uruguay | [Commission Implementing Decision 2012/484/EU](https://eur-lex.europa.eu/legal-content/EN/TXT/?uri=CELEX:32012D0484) of 21 August 2012, Art. 1(1), in force under Art. 45(9) | OJ L 227, 23.8.2012, p. 11 | 21 August 2012 (adoption date, see note) | no end date | none | none |
| US (via `dpf`) | United States | [Commission Implementing Decision (EU) 2023/1795](https://eur-lex.europa.eu/legal-content/EN/TXT/?uri=CELEX:32023D1795) of 10 July 2023, Art. 1 | OJ L 231, 20.9.2023, p. 118 | 10 July 2023 (adoption date, see note) | no end date | Its Article 1 covers only personal data transferred to organisations in the United States that are included in the 'Data Privacy Framework List' maintained by the U.S. Department of Commerce. | `dpf` with the importer's certification (see the transfer rules) |

Start dates marked (adoption date, see note): the decision sets no date from which it applies; it is addressed to the Member States and takes effect on notification, which its Official Journal text does not date, so the tool reads it as applying from its date of adoption (interpretation). With a `review_date`, a decision does not cover a transfer before the date it applies from or after its last day of validity, and a review date before an amendment that changed its scope or validity sends the transfer to review (`HIGH`, or the safeguard question where a safeguard is recorded): an amending act that sets no date from which it applies takes effect on notification, which its Official Journal text does not date, so the tool dates the amendment by its adoption. A review date after 2026-11-14 gets a note that later Commission acts are not reflected.

Decisions adopted under Article 25(6) of Directive 95/46/EC stay in force under Art. 45(9) GDPR until amended, replaced or repealed; their findings cite Art. 45(9) too. Implementing Decision (EU) 2016/2295 replaced their articles on suspending data flows and on monitoring and left Article 1 unchanged. The US decision is reached through the `dpf` mechanism, with the importer's certification, so the US is not on the adequacy list. The European Patent Organisation (`EPO`) is an international organisation with its seat in Munich: a transfer to it is a transfer under Chapter V (Art. 44), so the EEA exemption does not apply. The United Kingdom decisions under Directive (EU) 2016/680 (law enforcement) are outside the tool's GDPR scope.

### Scope conditions

Each condition reads one fact about the importer, recorded per destination under `transfers` or on a sub-processor entry ([input-format.md](input-format.md)). A value in the covered column meets the condition and one in the not-covered column fails it; any other value, or no value, leaves it unresolved, which never counts as adequacy. An interpretation maps the input's categories onto the decision's text and is repeated in a finding it decides.

| Destination | Fact | Provision | Requirement | Covered | Not covered | Interpretation |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| CA | `recipient_type` | Art. 1 and recital 5 | the importer must be subject to the Personal Information Protection and Electronic Documents Act | `"private_commercial"` | `"public_body"` | recital 5 says that the Act applies to private sector organisations acting in the course of commercial activities, not to organisations under the Federal Privacy Act or regulated by the public sector at a provincial level, nor to non-profit organisations and charitable activities unless they are of a commercial nature; the tool reads a private commercial organisation as covered, a public body as not covered and a non-profit as unresolved. It does not model recital 5's statement that the Act does not cover employment data used for non-commercial purposes other than that relating to employees in the federally regulated private sector, or the exemptions for organisations under substantially similar provincial laws (recital 6). |
| IL | `automated_processing` | Art. 1(1) | the transfer must be automated or, where it is not, the data must be subject to further automated processing in the State of Israel | `true` | `false` | none |
| JP | `recipient_type` | Art. 1(1) and recitals 32 and 33 | the importer must be a personal information handling business operator subject to the Act on the Protection of Personal Information | `"non_profit"`, `"private_commercial"` | `"public_body"` | recital 32 excludes the government and administrative agencies at central and local level from the definition of a personal information handling business operator, and recital 33 reads 'business' to include not-for-profit activities; the tool reads a private commercial organisation and a non-profit as business operators and a public body as not covered. |
| JP | `scope_carve_out` | Art. 1(2) | the importer must fall within none of the categories of Art. 1(2)(a) to (e) (press organisations, persons engaged in professional writing, academic organisations, religious bodies and political bodies, each to the extent of the purposes listed there) | `"none"` | `"applies"` | none |
| KR | `scope_carve_out` | Art. 1(2) | the importer must fall within none of the categories of Art. 1(2)(a) to (c) (religious organisations for their missionary activities, political parties for the nomination of candidates, and entities overseen by the Financial Services Commission for personal credit information under the Credit Information Act) | `"none"` | `"applies"` | none |

Uruguay: the decision's title refers to automated processing of personal data, but its Article 1(1) sets no such limit, and the tool follows Article 1(1) (interpretation). Brazil: the input records no fact for this limit, and the tool reads every importer in Brazil as a controller or processor subject to the LGPD, public or private (recitals 25 and 26); the exemptions from the LGPD the decision describes from recital 30 are not modelled (interpretation). Faroe Islands: the input records no fact for this limit, and the tool reads every recipient in the Faroe Islands as subject to the Faeroese Act (interpretation). Israel: the input records no fact for the limit of Article 2, and the tool reads every importer as located in the State of Israel as defined in accordance with international law (interpretation).
